question: Article 59 of Directive 2001/83/EC1 requires the package leaflet to list excipients, while Article 54 requires certain excipients to be listed on the outer packaging. However, neither provision requires disclosure of the species from which the product is derived. Excipients such as gelatine, stearates or lactose may be animal- or plant-derived, but this is not specified.

In correspondence with a citizen (Ares(2025)10521900; Ares(2026)1090942), the Commission confirmed that EU law does not require disclosure of species origin, while acknowledging the importance of informed patient choice based on ethical, cultural or religious considerations. This lack of transparency affects citizens who follow dietary restrictions related to animal products (e.g.

, halal, kosher, Hindu, vegetarian or vegan diets). Unlike food labelling rules, EU pharmaceutical legislation provides no mechanism to identify the origin of excipients, despite manufacturers already holding this information for quality and supply-chain purposes.
Other jurisdictions have taken steps in this direction: Switzerland requires disclosure for certain excipients, and the American Medical Association supports such transparency. 1.
Does the Commission plan to amend Directive 2001/83/EC or introduce other measures to require disclosure of the species from which excipients originate?
Has it assessed integrating this information into digital product information or eleaflets?
What costs does it foresee, given that this information is already available to manufacturers?
Directive 2001/83/EC of 6 November 2001 on the Community code relating to medicinal products for human use (ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2001/83/oj). 1
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (10.11.2026) Under the current EU pharmaceutical legislation, as well as under the new pharmaceutical legislation, there is no general obligation to indicate on the labelling or in the package leaflet the animal species from which an excipient is derived. Excipients need to be declared where this is required for the safe and appropriate use of the medicinal product.

At the same time, excipients of animal origin are subject to assessment in the context of the marketing authorisation procedure. Applicants must provide the competent authorities with the relevant information on the quality, safety and control of such materials and, where relevant, on their origin.

Although at the moment there are no plans and related assessments ongoing to amend the recently revised legislation so as to to require disclosure of the species from which excipients originate on the package leaflets, patients can receive information on the origin of excipients.

All assessment reports including information related to the human and animal origin of the excipients are available on the website of the European Medicines Agency for medicines authorised centrally, or on the websites of national competent authorities for medicines authorised nationally. This information helps patients and healthcare professionals to choose the appropriate medicinal product.
